catalog_quote: Kadu is one of the many tonal languages spoken in Southeast Asia. ... The Kadu language tonal system falls into the first category. The three tonemic distinctions occurring in Kadu involve three pitch registers. ... This thesis proposes that Kadu has phonemic contrasts between high, mid, and low tones occurring on all vowels and on all syllable types. ... Mid tone is the most common tone in this language. ... This section presents two types of syllable structures attested in Kadu: major and minor (also called strong and weak) syllables. Major syllables are those capable of functioning as major word classes such as nouns and verbs. The major syllables have more complex nuclei and contrastive tones. However, minor syllables cannot function alone but must combine with some other major syllable and must always precede the major syllable. ... Minor syllables may have a wide range of consonan…

tone_statements.citation: Huziwara, Keisuke. 2020. On the genetic position of Chakpa within Luish languages. Himalayan Linguistics 19(2): 44–55. DOI 10.5070/H91150999 (eScholarship, CC BY-NC-ND, open access).
tone_statements.quote: 2.2.4 Tones Proto-Luish had two distinctive tones. Cak/Sak also retains this two-tone system. Ganan developed the third tone (low tone), in which the original low tone became the secondary low tone after the high tone. Kadu also developed the third tone (low tone), from which emerged the fourth tone (creaky tone) in Setto and Molang varieties.

tone_statements.summary: Kadu: H vs (M/L/creaky) < PLu *H/*L; 3 tones, 4 in Setto/Molang; Ganan 3 (H, M, L).

tone_statements.translation: (1) a. Tone notation: ´ marks high tone (H), ` low tone (L), ˆ falling tone (F). The unmarked mid tone (M) carries no accent mark. b. The low tone in K[adu] and G[anan] is, in principle, what arose when a mid tone after a high tone changed. Words that begin with a low tone show that there once was a high-toned prefix. c. The falling tone in K arises from HM or ML having changed, and in principle appears only in MF forms. … (12) [Hypothesis 3] Forms deriving from PTB *@y or *@w correspond in Ganan, when they are not high-toned, to forms with an added glottal stop.
tone_statements.summary: Transcribes Ganan and Kadu with high, low and unmarked mid tone (Kadu also a falling tone, from HM/ML); low said to come from mid after high; Ganan adds a final glottal stop only off high tone.

sources.quote: '声調：四声調（高声調、中声調、低声調、下降（緊喉）声調）であり、固有の声調をもたない軽声として /ə/ がある。軽声は開音節のみであらわれるけれども、語の最終音節にはあらわれない。他の声調は、すべての音節構造であらわれうる。' [Tone: four tones (high, mid, low, falling/creaky), plus a light syllable /ə/ with no inherent tone; the light syllable occurs only in open syllables and never word-finally; the other tones can occur on every syllable type.] No stress statement.
sources.locator: abstract item 2 p. 47; sec. 2.2 item c p. 50 (p. 4)
sources.note: Most recent phonology of a Kadu variety (Molang); explicit statement that /ə/ light syllable has no inherent tone and never occurs word-finally — confirms sesquisyllabic tonal profile with no stress rule.

sources.note: The secondary syllable-final glottal stop of Ganan (vs open -i/-u in Cak and Kadu) is added only when the Proto-Luish rhyme was *iy/*uw AND the syllable does not carry high tone — a tone-conditioned sound change, so it presupposes the Ganan/Kadu tone categories.

sources.note: Sec. 4.1.1 (pp. 26-27) is a secondhand Kadu phonological sketch from Sangdong 2012 and Huziwara (p.c. 2012): three tones HIGH 55~44~45, MID 33~22 (lexically the most common), LOW 22~11 with minimal triplets (sín/sīn/sìn, há/hā/hà, káp/kāp/kàp), plus Huziwara's observation that the three-way contrast also occurs in stopped syllables; Kadu is 'highly sesquisyllabic'. In the Jingpho/Luish cognate notes (Appendix III, pp. 85-90) Kadu-Sak tone mismatches are flagged for individual etyma ('raw/unripe', 'cheek', 'scale'), not asserted as a general non-correspondence.

tone.quote: 各言語の音韻論について詳細は藤原［2008, 2012a, 2013a］を参照。 … 同源形式と推定されるけれども、声調などが通則にあわないことがある。その ようなばあい、再構形式に?をつける。たとえば（96）‘peck (v)’ PL *hru?。 … 高声調をもつ接頭辞は右肩に H をつけてしめす。たとえば（95）‘pain (vi)’ PL *kH -na。 … (64) ‘gong’ PL *CH -moN; C moN, K (máuN), G màuN; WrB {mong’:}, M mÓN; PTB — 注 K は声調から判断してビルマ語からの借用語であるけれども、G は声調から 判断して借用語ではないと推定される。
tone.locator: p. 2 n. 4; p. 5 sec. 2.4 表記上の注意 (bullets on 声調 and 高声調 prefixes); p. 14 Appendix 1 set (64) 'gong' note
tone.translation: For details of the phonology of each language see Huziwara [2008, 2012a, 2013a]. … Some forms are presumed cognate although their tones etc. do not follow the regular correspondences; in such cases a ? is added to the reconstructed form, e.g. (96) 'peck (v)' PL *hru?. … A prefix bearing high tone is shown with a superscript H, e.g. (95) 'pain (vi)' PL *kH-na. … (64) 'gong' PL *CH-moN; C moN, K (máuN), G màuN; WrB {mong':}, M mÓN; PTB — Note: K[adu], judging from its tone, is a loanword from Burmese, but G[anan], judging from its tone, is presumed not to be a loanword.
tone.summary: Comparative Proto-Luish study; Mawteik Kadu forms carry high/low tone marks and notes flag irregular tone correspondences, but Kadu's tone inventory is not described (refers to Huziwara 2013).
tone.says: Comparative Proto-Luish study; Mawteik Kadu forms carry high/low tone marks and notes flag irregular tone correspondences, but Kadu's tone inventory is not described (refers to Huziwara 2013).
